title: SynchronizationContext
sub: Who runs the code after await
cards/0/body:
SynchronizationContext is an object with a Post(callback) method: "run this where it belongs". A thread's current context lives in SynchronizationContext.Current.

  • WPF has DispatcherSynchronizationContext, WinForms has WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext: Post puts the callback into the UI thread's message queue.
  • Unity has UnitySynchronizationContext: Post puts the callback into a queue that the main thread drains every frame.
  • A console app and ASP.NET Core: Current == null. Pool threads have no context either, even if Task.Run was called from a window.
cards/1/title: What await does with the context
cards/1/body:
At the pause, await reads SynchronizationContext.Current and remembers it.

If there is a context, then when the task completes the continuation is sent there with Post and runs on the UI thread. That's why a handler can touch controls after await: from any other thread, WPF would throw InvalidOperationException.

If there is no context, the continuation runs on a pool thread.
cards/2/task: Run the scenario in WPF, then switch to a console app and see who runs the continuations.
cards/3/q: Why can a WPF handler write label.Text = … after await?
cards/3/options/0: await captured the UI thread's context, and the continuation arrived there via Post
cards/3/options/1: WPF lets you change controls from any thread
cards/3/options/2: await blocks the UI thread until the response, so the code never leaves it
cards/3/explain: At the await, SynchronizationContext.Current is a DispatcherSynchronizationContext. The continuation went to the UI thread's queue and ran there.
cards/4/q: Where does the main thread have a SynchronizationContext by default? Select all that apply.
cards/4/explain: In a console app and ASP.NET Core, SynchronizationContext.Current == null, so the pool runs the continuations.
cards/5/body:
Post runs nothing by itself: it only puts the callback into a queue. The UI thread has one queue for everything (clicks, repaints, continuations after await), and the UI thread works through it one item at a time.

If the UI thread is busy with a long computation or blocked, the queue stalls: neither clicks nor continuations run.
cards/6/q: The UI thread is busy with a long computation, and a continuation after await is already in its queue. When will it run?
cards/6/options/0: When the UI thread finishes the computation and reaches it in the queue
cards/6/options/1: Right away, on a free pool thread
cards/6/explain: The continuation waits its turn, just like clicks: only the UI thread can run it.
cards/7/body:
If SynchronizationContext.Current == null, await also checks the current TaskScheduler. By default that's the thread pool.

More precisely: without a context the continuation usually runs synchronously on the thread that completed the task, for example the pool thread that got the OS notification that the response arrived. If it can't run right away (for instance, the task has the RunContinuationsAsynchronously flag), it goes into the pool's queue.
cards/7/deep: SynchronizationContext.Current and TaskScheduler.Current are checked at the moment of the await. You install your own context with SynchronizationContext.SetSynchronizationContext; that's how Unity and libraries such as AsyncContext from Nito.AsyncEx run every continuation on a single thread.
cards/8/q: In a WPF handler: await Task.Run(async () => { await LoadAsync(); label.Text = "ok"; }); What happens on the label.Text line?
cards/8/options/0: InvalidOperationException: there's no context inside Task.Run, so a pool thread runs the continuation
cards/8/options/1: It's fine: Task.Run was started from the UI thread, so await returns there
cards/8/explain: The await inside the lambda reads the pool thread's SynchronizationContext.Current, which is null. The handler's context doesn't matter here: only the outer await would capture it.
cards/9/q: Match each environment to its SynchronizationContext
cards/10/q: How does ExecutionContext differ from SynchronizationContext?
cards/10/options/0: ExecutionContext is data (AsyncLocal, culture) that rides with the continuation; SynchronizationContext is where the continuation itself is sent
cards/10/options/1: They're the same thing under two names
cards/10/options/2: ExecutionContext decides which thread resumes, and SynchronizationContext carries AsyncLocal
cards/10/explain: ExecutionContext is always captured and restored. SynchronizationContext only decides who runs the continuation: the UI thread via Post, or the pool.
